'''Grete Hermann''' (2 March 1901 – 15 April 1984) was a German mathematician, philosopher, [[Theoretical physicists|theoretical physicist]], writer, and educator. She is known for her foundational work in quantum mechanics and [[computer algebra]]; her writings on [[political philosophy]]; and her work with the [[Internationaler Sozialistischer Kampfbund]] (ISK) in opposition to Nazism. 

Hermann worked on reconciling the [[neo-Kantianism|neo-Kantian]] conception of causality with quantum mechanics. This work led to her critique of [[Von Neumann's no hidden variables proof]]. Her criticism was long ignored; it was discovered in 1974 by [[Max Jammer]] who publicized it. In 1936, Hermann shared in the award of the [[Richard Avenarius]] prize. She was the first graduate student of [[Emmy Noether]] and she published the posthumous works of others, including that of [[Leonard Nelson]]. 

Between 1927 and 1940, Hermann published a number of anti-Nazi articles under various pseudonyms in ''[[Der Funke]]'' and ''[[Sozialistische Warte]]'', publications edited by [[Willi Eichler]]. Due to her involvement with the ISK, Hermann had to flee Nazi Germany until the conclusion of World War II. During her exile, she was a leader of the [[Union of German Socialist Organisations in Great Britain]].

In her later years, she co-founded the philosophical journal [[Ratio (journal)|''Ratio'']], where she was a member of the editorial board until her death. She also became the first head at the {{Ill|Pädagogische Hochschule Bremen|lt=Bremen Pedagogical University|de}}, a teacher education university, which later integrated into the University of Bremen after her retirement. After the death of [[Minna Specht]], with whom she worked and lived for many years, she took over leadership of {{Ill|Philosophisch-Politische Akademie|de}} and became withdrawn from public life, focused on [[critical philosophy]] and refining Nelsonian ethics. She died in 1984 in [[Bremen]].

== Early life and education ==
Hermann was born in [[Bremen]], where her father Gerhard Heinrich Hermann<ref name=":5" /> was a merchant sailor officer for [[Norddeutscher Lloyd]] who also co-owned a stonework factory.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Abele |first=Andrea E. |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-0348-7963-7 |title=Traumjob Mathematik! |last2=Neunzert |first2=Helmut |last3=Tobies |first3=Renate |date=2004 |publisher=Birkhäuser Basel |isbn=978-3-7643-6749-7 |location=Basel |language=de |doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-7963-7}}</ref> Her mother Clara Auguste {{Nee|Leipoldt}}<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Schumacher |first=M. |last2=Schöneberg |first2=R. |last3=Flammersfeld |first3=A. |date=1966 |title=Der Zerfall des Pt191 |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01330550 |journal=Zeitschrift für Physik |language=de |volume=191 |issue=4 |pages=343–353 |doi=10.1007/BF01330550 |issn=1434-6001|url-access=subscription }}</ref> was dedicated to religious studies.<ref name=":1" /> Hermann had a very close relationship with her mother.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=258|pages=}} Both of her grandfathers were [[pastor]]s.<ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Venz |first=Vera |title=Zur Biographie von Grete Hermann |publisher=Grin Verlag |year=2009 |isbn=978-3-640-41192-4 |location=Germany |language=de}}</ref> She took piano lessons.<ref name=":6" /> Her father abandoned the family and his work to become a wandering "itinerant preacher" in 1921.<ref name=":1" /> She was raised in a middle-class [[Protestantism in Germany|Protestant]] family<ref name=":12" /> with two sisters and four brothers,<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 March 2017 |title=Henry-Hermann, Grete (1901–1984) |url=https://bremer-frauenmuseum.de/2017/03/21/henry-hermann-grete1/ |access-date=2 January 2026 |website=Bremer Frauenmuseum e.V. |language=de |archive-date=9 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251009073831/https://bremer-frauenmuseum.de/2017/03/21/henry-hermann-grete1/ |url-status=live }}</ref> including physicist [[Carl H. Hermann]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Herrmann |first=Kay |chapter=Brief 8: Grete Hermann an ihre Mutter [Auguste Hermann (geb. Leipoldt)] über ihre Gespräche mit Heisenberg in Leipzig und andere philosophische Arbeitsberichte (5.3.1934) |date=2019 |title=Grete Henry-Hermann: Philosophie – Mathematik – Quantenmechanik |pages=463–463 |editor-last=Herrmann |editor-first=Kay |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-658-16241-2_30 |access-date=3 January 2026 |place=Wiesbaden |publisher=Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden |language=de |doi=10.1007/978-3-658-16241-2_30 |isbn=978-3-658-16240-5|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Carl H. Hermann |url=https://www.iucr.org/publ/50yearsofxraydiffraction/full-text/hermann |access-date=3 January 2026 |website=www.iucr.org |archive-date=24 July 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220724052818/https://www.iucr.org/publ/50yearsofxraydiffraction/full-text/hermann |url-status=live }}</ref> 

She was one of few girls admitted by exception<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=18}} to {{Ill|Oberschule am Barkhof|de}},<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=22 April 2025 |title=Grete Hermann: the quantum physicist who challenged Werner Heisenberg and John von Neumann |url=https://physicsworld.com/grete-hermann-the-quantum-physicist-who-challenged-werner-heisenberg-and-john-von-neumann/ |access-date=31 December 2025 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> which did not become co-educational until 1953.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Detailseite - Archivportal-D |url=https://www.archivportal-d.de/item/NUO3EKGY4PHS2K4LJWLXLUEHA6KAGTYA |access-date=3 January 2026 |website=www.archivportal-d.de |archive-date=15 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230115173416/https://www.archivportal-d.de/item/NUO3EKGY4PHS2K4LJWLXLUEHA6KAGTYA |url-status=live }}</ref> After graduating in 1920,<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last=Reichenberger |first=Andrea |date=1 September 2024 |title=Grete Hermann's ethical philosophy of physics |url=https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/grete-hermanns-ethical-philosophy-of-physics |journal=Physics Today |language=en |volume=77 |issue=9 |pages=44–50 |doi=10.1063/pt.etra.qcce |issn=0031-9228|doi-access=free }}</ref> she took the exam to become a teacher there.<ref name=":1" /> However, she instead enrolled at the [[University of Göttingen]] in 1921 with her two older brothers,<ref name=":6" />{{Reference page|page=109|pages=}}  to study [[Mathematics]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Peijnenburg |first=Adriana Johanna Maria |title=Women in the history of analytic philosophy: selected papers of the Tilburg – Groningen Conference, 2019 |last2=Verhaegh |first2=Alexander Alfons |date=2022 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-031-08593-2 |series=Women in the history of philosophy and sciences |location=Cham}}</ref> 

At Göttingen, Hermann was the first student of mathematician [[Emmy Noether]]. She also studied under [[Edmund Landau]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reichenberger |first=Andrea |date=2020 |title=Grete Hermann – Between Physics and Philosophy Edited by Elise Crull and Guido Bacciagaluppi: SPRINGER, 2016, STUDIES IN HISTORY AND PHILOSOPHY OF SCIENCE VOLUME 42, XV + 281 PP., $119.99, ISBN 978-94-024-0968-0 |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00283-020-09978-w |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=80–82 |doi=10.1007/s00283-020-09978-w |issn=0343-6993|doi-access=free }}</ref> She defended her thesis in 1925, which included her majors of study.<ref name=":1" /> She was awarded her [[Doctor of Philosophy]] (PhD) in Mathematics with minors in [[Philosophy]] and [[Physics]].<ref name=":4" /> Her thesis was published in 1926 in ''[[Mathematische Annalen]]'' and incorporated the work of [[Kurt Hentzelt]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hermann |first=Grete |date=1926 |title=Die Frage der endlich vielen Schritte in der Theorie der Polynomideale: Unter Benutzung nachgelassener Sätze von K. Hentzelt |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01206635 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |language=de |volume=95 |issue=1 |pages=736–788 |doi=10.1007/BF01206635 |issn=0025-5831|url-access=subscription }}</ref> a student of Noether and [[Ernst Sigismund Fischer]] at the [[University of Erlangen–Nuremberg|University of Erlangen]] who died in WWI.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Magnaghi-Delfino |first=Paola |title=Faces of Geometry: II Edition |date=2021 |publisher=Springer International Publishing AG |others=Giampiero Mele, Tullia Norando |isbn=978-3-030-63701-9 |series=Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems Ser |location=Cham}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Rowe |first=David E. |author-link=David E. Rowe |chapter=Max and Emmy Noether: Mathematics in Erlangen |date=2021 |title=Emmy Noether – Mathematician Extraordinaire |pages=1–38 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-63810-8_1 |access-date=31 December 2025 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-63810-8_1 |isbn=978-3-030-63809-2|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Hermann published Hentzelt's theorems after his death.<ref name=":6" /> After obtaining her PhD, she studied at the [[University of Freiburg]].<ref name=":13" />

Her PhD thesis, ''The Question of Finitely Many Steps in Polynomial Ideal Theory'' ({{Langx|de|Die Frage der endlich vielen Schritte in der Theorie der Polynomideale}}) is the foundational paper for modern [[computer algebra]]. It first established the existence of [[algorithms]] (including [[computational complexity|complexity]] bounds) for many of the basic problems of [[abstract algebra]], such as [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] membership for [[polynomial ring]]s. Hermann's algorithm for [[primary decomposition]] is used in modern computing.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.springer.com/us/book/9781402000041 |title=Applications of Algebraic Geometry to Coding Theory, Physics and Computation |date=2001 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-94-010-1011-5 |editor1-last=Ciliberto |editor1-first=Ciro |editor1-link=Ciro Ciliberto |series=Nato Science Series II |location=Dordrecht |language=en |editor2-last=Hirzebruch |editor2-first=Friedrich |editor3-last=Miranda |editor3-first=Rick |editor4-last=Teicher |editor4-first=Mina |editor4-link=Mina Teicher |archive-date=20 September 2017 |access-date=29 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170920190643/https://www.springer.com/us/book/9781402000041 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Academia and research ==

=== Theoretical physics ===
In 1934, Hermann went to [[Leipzig]] "for the express purpose of reconciling a [[neo-Kantianism|neo-Kantian]] conception of causality with the new quantum mechanics". In Leipzig, many exchanges of thoughts took place among Hermann, [[Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker]], and [[Werner Heisenberg]].<ref name="HSP">{{cite journal |last1=Bacciagaluppi |first1=Guido |last2=Crull |first2=Elise |author2-link=Elise Crull |date=December 2009 |title=Heisenberg (and Schrödinger, and Pauli) on hidden variables |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=374–382 |bibcode=2009SHPMP..40..374B |doi=10.1016/j.shpsb.2009.08.004 |s2cid=13140289 |id=PhilSci:[https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/4759 4759]}}</ref> In these discussions, she argued that Kantian causality should remain secure, and questioned whether quantum uncertainty reflected subjective ignorance or a principled limit requiring a revision of the Kantian framework.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Heisenberg |first=Werner |title=Physics and beyond: encounters and conversations |date=1972 |publisher=Harper & Row |isbn=978-0-06-131622-7 |series=Harper torchbooks |location=New York}}</ref> The contents of her work in this time, including a focus on a distinction of [[predictability]] and [[causality]], are known from three of her own publications,<ref name="soler">{{Cite book |last1=Soler |first1=Léna |title=Constituting Objectivity |publisher=Springer |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4020-9509-2 |editor=M. Bitbol |series=The Western Ontario Series in Philosophy of Science |volume=74 |pages=329–344 |chapter=The Convergence of Transcendental Philosophy and Quantum Physics: Grete Henry-Hermann's 1935 Pioneering Proposal |doi=10.1007/978-1-4020-9510-8_20 |editor2=P. Kerszberg |editor3=J. Petitot}}</ref> and from later description of their discussions by von Weizsäcker,<ref>Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, see for example: [[Jagdish Mehra]], [[Helmut Rechenberg]]: ''The Historical Development of Quantum Theory'', Volume 6 ''The Completion of Quantum Mechanics 1926–1941'', Part 2, Springer, 2001, {{ISBN|0-387-95086-9}}, [https://books.google.com/books?id=kn6mb0ltm0UC&pg=PA712 p. 712 f.]</ref> and the discussion of Hermann's work in chapter ten of Heisenberg's ''[[Physics and Beyond]]''.<ref name=":3" /> Heisenberg describes her as dissatisfied with intermediate positions, but as partly reassured by replies influenced by [[Niels Bohr]], and presents the exchange as clarifying the relation between Kantian concepts and [[modern physics]].<ref name=":2" /> 

From Denmark, she published her work ''The foundations of quantum mechanics in the philosophy of nature'' ({{Langx|de|Die naturphilosophischen Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik}}). This work has been referred to as "one of the earliest and best philosophical treatments of the new quantum mechanics".<ref name=":3">{{Cite book| last1=Crull |first1=Elise|author1-link=Elise Crull|last2=Bacciagaluppi|first2=Guido | chapter=Translation of: W. Heisenberg, "Ist eine deterministische Ergänzung der Quantenmechanik möglich?|title=The Einstein Paradox: The Debate on Nonlocality and Incompleteness in 1935|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2021|id=PhilSci:[https://philsci-archive.pitt.edu/8590 8590]}}</ref> In this work, she concludes:<ref>Grete Hermann: ''The foundations of quantum mechanics in the philosophy of nature''. Cited after its translation from German with an introduction by Dirk Lumma in ''The Harvard Review of Philosophy VII'' (1999), [https://www.pdcnet.org/8525737F00588A37/file/6AEBF8E4AC66DA51852577CA005F4EF1/$FILE/harvardreview_1999_0007_0001_0035_0044.pdf p. 35 ff.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231118062939/https://www.pdcnet.org/8525737F00588A37/file/6AEBF8E4AC66DA51852577CA005F4EF1/$FILE/harvardreview_1999_0007_0001_0035_0044.pdf |date=18 November 2023 }}</ref>

{{Blockquote|The theory of quantum mechanics forces us […] to drop the assumption of the absolute character of knowledge about nature, and to deal with the principle of causality independently of this assumption. Quantum mechanics has therefore not contradicted the law of causality at all, but has clarified it and has removed from it other principles which are not necessarily connected to it.||}}

In June 1936, Hermann was awarded the [[Richard Avenarius]] prize together with [[Eduard May]] and Th. Vogel.<ref>C. F. Freiherr v. Weizsäcker (interviewed), Konrad Lindner: ''Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker über sein Studium in Leipzig'', NTM Zeitschrift für Geschichte der Wissenschaften, Technik und Medizin, vol.&nbsp;1, no.&nbsp;1, pp.&nbsp;3–18, {{doi|10.1007/BF02914089}}, see fulltext</ref><ref>V. F. Lenzen: ''Die Bedeutung der Modernen Physik für die Theorie der Erkenntnis. Drei mit dem Richard Avenarius-Preis ausgezeichnete Arbeiten von Dr. Grete Hermann, Dr. E. May, Dr. Th. Vogel'', In A. P. Ushenko (ed.): ''The Philosophy of Relativity'', Science, vol.&nbsp;85, no.&nbsp;2217 (25 June 1937), pp. 606–607</ref>

==== Hidden variables ====
Based on her views on quantum causality, Hermann concluded that there was no way to explain quantum mechanics in terms of a [[hidden variable theory]]. However, she published a critique of [[John von Neumann]]'s 1932 proof from his book ''[[Mathematical Foundations of Quantum Mechanics]]'', that was widely claimed to show that such a theory was impossible. Hermann's work on this subject went unnoticed by the physics community until it was independently discovered and published by [[John Stewart Bell]] in 1966, and her earlier discovery was pointed out by [[Max Jammer]] in 1974.<ref>{{cite book|first=Max |last=Jammer |author-link=Max Jammer |title=The Philosophy of Quantum Mechanics |pages=207–209,265–274 |year=1974 |publisher=John Wiley and Sons |isbn=0-471-43958-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mermin |first1=N. David |author-link1=N. David Mermin |last2=Schack |first2=Rüdiger |date=September 2018 |title=Homer Nodded: Von Neumann's Surprising Oversight |journal=Foundations of Physics |language=en |volume=48 |issue=9 |pages=1007–1020 |arxiv=1805.10311 |bibcode=2018FoPh...48.1007M |doi=10.1007/s10701-018-0197-5 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Some have posited that had her critique not remained nearly unknown for decades, her ideas would have put in question the unequivocal acceptance of the [[Copenhagen interpretation]] of quantum mechanics, by providing a credible basis for the further development of nonlocal hidden variable theories, which would have changed the historical development of quantum mechanics.<ref name="soler"/>

=== Pedagogy ===
During the period of Nazi Germany, Hermann was in exile in Denmark and Britain as a member of [[Internationaler Sozialistischer Kampfbund]] (ISK), an anti-Nazi political organization.<ref name=":9" /> During this time, she visited Germany and France in secret to continue her research.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28|pages=}} Her first position upon her return to Germany was at a secondary school for girls in [[Karlsruhe]] teaching mathematics, where she remained until October 1949, when she was appointed the first provisional head at the {{Ill|Pädagogische Hochschule Bremen|lt=Bremen Pedagogical University|de}} (BPU), a teacher education university. She was denied a professorship due to her British citizenship, which had nullified her German citizenship. The senator for schools and education, {{Ill|Christian Paulmann|de}}, advocated for her German citizenship to be restored so she could become a professor in Bremen, arguing that she had proved herself by rejecting appointments at [[Marburg University]] and the [[University of Tübingen]], after which she was awarded [[dual citizenship]]. She became a full professor in July 1950, and she requested to step down to deputy head.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=30}} While there, she was accused of indoctrinating the college toward [[Marxism]] and [[materialism]] by the [[Christian Democratic Union of Germany]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Brückmann |first=Asmut |date=13 April 2014 |title=Da staunte der Nobelpreisträger |newspaper=Weser-Kurier |pages=W8 |language=de}}</ref> During her tenure until 1966, and into her retirement, she supported its transformation into a full university. BPU integrated into the [[University of Bremen]] between 1971 and 1973.<ref name=":9" /> After she retired, she withdrew from academia aside from [[critical philosophy]].<ref name=":12" />

=== Philosophy ===
Hermann worked as an assistant for [[Leonard Nelson]], a German mathematician and philosopher in the [[Neo-Friesian school|Neo-Friesian]] school of thought, beginning in 1925.<ref name="soler" /> She was skeptical of Nelson's rigidity, finding many of his rules to be restrictive of free thought.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=|pages=23–24}} When her mother fell ill, Nelson discouraged her from visiting her bedside, due to the Nelsonian ideal of prioritizing political matters over private ones. As a result, Hermann did not see her mother before she died. She later wrote about this as an example of Nelson's inhumanity and ethical issues surrounding his philosophies.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=|pages=258–259}} When Nelson died in 1927, she continued to work on many of the problems he posed.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last=Heckmann |first=Gustav |date=December 1984 |title=Grete Henry-Hermann's Development of Leonard Nelson's Ethics |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_ratio_1984-12_26_2 |journal=Ratio |language=en |publisher=Wiley Subscription Services, Inc. |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=97–102 |issn= |via=Internet Archive}}</ref> In 1945, she published {{Lang|de|Politik und Ethik}} (English: ''Politics and Ethics''; published in 1947), a criticism of [[political apathy]] and the complicity of [[Perpetrators, victims, and bystanders|bystanders]] in [[The Holocaust]]. In it she concludes:<ref>{{cite book |last=Herrmann |first=Kay |chapter=Gedanken zum Abwägungsgesetz in der Ethik Leonard Nelsons |date=2023 |title=Grete Henry-Hermann: Sittlichkeit und Vernunft |pages=147–167 |editor-last=Herrmann |editor-first=Kay |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-658-41993-6_3 |place=Wiesbaden |publisher=Springer Fachmedien Wiesbaden |language=de |doi=10.1007/978-3-658-41993-6_3 |isbn=978-3-658-41992-9 |last2=Neißer |first2=Barbara |editor2-last=Neißer |editor2-first=Barbara|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{Reference page|page=33|pages=}} 

{{Blockquote|text=Whoever lives in the Third Reich or otherwise comes to terms with it, but isolates themselves from the political events around them in order to occupy themselves with other, in themselves beautiful and worthy subjects, is lending their name and their work to this system. There is no neutrality towards the legal and cultural decline in public life. Whoever does not oppose it is complicit in it. Whatever beautiful and good things they may create otherwise are devalued by this participation in the social injustice with which it is burdened.}}

In 1957, she co-founded the philosophical journal [[Ratio (journal)|''Ratio'']]. She remained a member of the editorial board until her death.<ref name=":13">{{cite journal |last=Heckmann |first=Gustav |date=December 1984 |title=In Memoriam: Grete Henry-Hermann |url=https://archive.org/details/sim_ratio_1984-12_26_2 |journal=Ratio |language=en |publisher=Wiley Subscription Services, Inc. |volume=26 |issue=2 |page=95 |via=Internet Archive}}</ref> After she retired from pedagogical work, she focused entirely on re-shaping Nelsonian thought with her ethics until nearly her death. In a letter in July 1983 she wrote:<ref name=":0" />{{Blockquote|I wish to understand by what modification the core of truth in Nelsonian philosophy can be freed from its misleading absolutist claims and its true meaning vindicated.||}}
In her paper {{Lang|de|Die Überwindung des Zufalls}} (English: ''Overcoming Contingency'';<ref name=":0" /> or ''Conquering Chance'' as published in 1991<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Henry‐Hermann |first=Grete |date=1991 |orig-date=1953 |editor-last=Winch |editor-first=Peter |title=Conquering Chance: Critical Reflections on Leonard Nelson's Establishment of Ethics as a Science |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9205.1991.tb00490.x |journal=Philosophical Investigations |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=1–80 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9205.1991.tb00490.x |issn=0190-0536|url-access=subscription }}</ref>)'','' a critical response to Nelson's work, she concludes that [[moral judgement]] is emergent from cooperation of reason and sensibility. Her thesis argued that aside from "mindless panic", there are no behaviors which arise solely from internal mental activity or external influences through the senses. This was directly in opposition to Nelson's belief that reason by itself could generate action, which was central to the absolutist foundation of Nelsonian ethical reason being uninfluenced by external stimuli. Hermann argued that repeated ethical behavior would not absolutely lead to predictable future actions in accordance with moral duty, and reliance on that belief led to complacency that resulted in allowing moral injustices to occur, or immoral actions. She wrote that moral behavior necessarily requires constant labor involving evaluation of the external environment and inner thoughts.<ref name=":0" /> 

[[Gustav Heckmann]], the philosopher who wrote her obituary in ''Ratio'',<ref name=":0" /> published her final (1984) paper {{Lang|de|Die Überwindung des Zufalls: Kritische Betrachtungen zu Leonard Nelsons Begründung der Ethik als Wissenschaft}} (English: ''Thoughts on the Principle of Fair Adjustment in the Ethics of Leonard Nelson'') posthumously in 1985.<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |last=Henry-Hermann |first=Grete |title=Die Überwindung des Zufalls: kritische Betrachtungen zu Leonard Nelsons Begründung der Ethik als Wissenschaft |date=1985 |publisher=Meiner |isbn=978-3-7873-0658-9 |editor-last=Heckmann |editor-first=Gustav |location=Hamburg |language=de |trans-title=Thoughts on the Principle of Fair Adjustment in the Ethics of Leonard Nelson |orig-date=1984}}</ref> In this work, Hermann refined her earlier works, in which she argued that spatial awareness was equally as important to understanding how people are motivated by personal interests because that motivation extends to the social world.<ref name=":0" /> She concludes that Kantian practical experience is a necessary component of the study of [[ethical decision-making]],<ref name=":14" /> which Heckmann explains to mean that our relationships with people and early [[socialization]] are necessarily part of how we govern our behaviors.<ref name=":0" />

== Politics and exile ==
Nelson co-founded ISK with [[Minna Specht]] in 1925, when Hermann began working for him.<ref name=":9" /> She waited to join ISK until after Nelson's death due to rules and demands he imposed on members that she perceived as threatening to her intellectual independence, including requiring members to adhere to vegetarianism and leave the church.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last=Crull |first=Elise |title=Grete Hermann - Between Physics and Philosophy |last2=Bacciagaluppi |first2=Guido |date=2017 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-94-024-0968-0 |series=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science |location=Dordrecht}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=|pages=23–24}} Specht was the director of {{Ill|Landerziehungsheim Walkemühle|de}}, a progressive school with adult political training, where Hermann took over some of Nelson's philosophy classes after he died.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=|pages=24–25}} The ISK was vehemently opposed to the Nazi Party<ref name=":9" /> and connected with the [[Quakers in Europe]], after Nelson encountered [[John Sturge Stephens]] and [[Norman Angell]] at Göttingen. Stephens introduced Nelson to [[Alfred Barratt Brown]], a Quaker and Principal at [[Ruskin College]], to build more support for ISK through the European Quaker and [[Pacifism|pacifist]] network in academia.<ref name=":10">{{Cite book |url=https://brill.com/view/title/34355 |title=Exile and Gender II: Politics, Education and the Arts |date=22 May 2017 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-04-34352-8 |editor-last=Brinson |editor-first=Charmian |doi=10.1163/9789004343528_008 |editor-last2=Buresova |editor-first2=Jana Barbora |editor-last3=Hammel |editor-first3=Andrea |archive-date=5 August 2022 |access-date=2 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220805122858/https://brill.com/view/title/34355 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{Reference page|page=8}} 

=== During World War II ===
After Nelson's death, she and Specht published Nelson's work ''System der philosophischen Ethik und Pädagogik'' in 1932.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=24|pages=}} [[Willi Eichler]] replaced Nelson as the leader of ISK and started a newspaper called ''[[Der Funke]]'', in which Hermann used several pseudonyms to publish articles denouncing [[Nazism]] and [[totalitarianism]].<ref name=":9" /> She,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Henry-Hermann |first=Grete |date=1986 |title=Die Überwindung des Zufalls. Kritische Betrachtungen Zu Leonard Nelsons Begründung der Ethik Als Wissenschaft |url=https://philpapers.org/rec/HENDBD-7 |journal=Journal for General Philosophy of Science / Zeitschrift für Allgemeine Wissenschaftstheorie |language=de |volume=17 |issue=2 |pages=384–386}}</ref> her brother Carl, and his wife [[Eva Hermann|Eva]] became critical of religion as [[Adolf Hitler]] began campaigning, joining the pacifist movement, and, in 1933,<ref>{{Cite web |last= |title=Eva Hermann |url=https://www.raoulwallenberg.net/saviors/german2/eva-hermann-654/ |access-date=2 January 2026 |website=The International Raoul Wallenberg Foundation |language=en-US |archive-date=17 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251117030600/https://www.raoulwallenberg.net/saviors/german2/eva-hermann-654/ |url-status=live }}</ref> at the onset of the [[Nazi persecution of Jews]], Carl and Eva joined the Quakers to help Jews escape.<ref name=":11">{{Cite book |last=Mordecai Paldiel |url=http://archive.org/details/pathofrighteousg00pald |title=The path of the righteous |date=1993 |publisher=Ktav |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-88125-376-4 |pages=154–155}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=154}} In March, as Hitler came into power, [[Waldmühlen|Walkemühle]] was occupied by [[Nazi Germany]], and the school was closed and cleared by Nazi forces. Hermann and Specht arranged for the important documents from the school to be preserved by Willi Warnke, who was intercepted by the Nazis and the documents confiscated.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=25|pages=}} Warnke was executed in 1938.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://codoh.com/wp-content/uploads/InconvenientHistory-Volume10-2018.pdf |title=Inconvenient History: A Quarterly Journal for Free Historical Inquiry |publisher=Academic Research Media Review Education Group Ltd |year=2024 |isbn=978-1-83640-010-3 |volume=10 |archive-date=26 November 2024 |access-date=2 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241126030738/https://codoh.com/wp-content/uploads/InconvenientHistory-Volume10-2018.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Carl and Eva were both arrested and jailed by the [[Nazi police]] for harboring a Jewish family in 1943.<ref name=":11" />{{Reference page|page=154}}

Between 1935 and 1940, Hermann contributed [[political philosophy]] works to a socialist periodical edited by Eichler in Paris called ''[[Sozialistische Warte]]'', under the pseudonyms Leonore Bremer, Gerda Bremer and Peter Ramme.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28}} Hermann fled Germany for Denmark in 1934, where she taught Socratic philosophy<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28}} at exile schools,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bacciagaluppi |first=Guido |date=2020 |title=Physics and Beyond: Essay review of Kay Herrmann (Ed.): Grete Henry-Hermann: Philosophie–Mathematik–Quantenmechanik. Springer: Wiesbaden 2019, xv + 663 pp. |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10838-020-09529-z |journal=Journal for General Philosophy of Science |language=en |volume=51 |issue=4 |pages=595–610 |doi=10.1007/s10838-020-09529-z |issn=0925-4560}}</ref> first on [[Funen]] with Specht, then in 1936 at [[Copenhagen]] in a school established by [[Gustav Heckmann]], with whom she lived. In 1937, she and Specht fled to Britain as the [[Nazi occupation of Denmark]] began.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=|pages=27–28}} [[Peter Scott (social entrepreneur)|Peter Scott]], a Quaker who founded the [[Brynmawr Experiment]] and who was connected with ISK, offered to house the school at the settlement in [[Wales]],<ref name=":10" />{{Reference page|page=7}} so Hermann, Specht, and the other teachers moved the school there. However, due to [[Defence Regulation 18B]], teachers began to be captured and placed in [[internment camp]]s, the school soon closed<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=246}} and Hermann and Specht relocated to London in 1938.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28}} 

In London, she met Edward Henry, a technician<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28}} and member of the [[Socialist Vanguard Group]], the British arm of ISK.<ref name=":10" />{{Reference page|page=90}} They married in February 1938.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28}} At the time, it was nearly impossible for German exiles to obtain work permits, so many refugee women married to be automatically granted British citizenship.<ref name=":10" />{{Reference page|page=15}} Thus, the marriage was classified as a [[marriage of convenience]] that protected her from internment<ref name=":9" /> due to Nazi persecution.<ref name=":10" />{{Reference page|page=90}} She resided with Specht. In a letter in a 1946 job application to train teachers at {{Ill|Schule an der Vegesacker Straße|de}}, she stated she was not bound by her marriage, and urgently wished to help reconstruct Germany.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=28}} While in London, Hermann and Specht were leaders of the [[Union of German Socialist Organisations in Great Britain]].<ref name=":9" />

=== Post World War II ===
After [[World War II]] ended, in 1946, she divorced Henry,<ref name=":10" />{{Reference page|page=90}} joined the [[Social Democratic Party of Germany|Social Democratic Party]] (SPD), and returned to what would become [[West Germany]].<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":6" /> She then combined her interests in physics and mathematics with political philosophy. She became critical of [[Philosophy of science|Western scientific inquiry]], which she felt was one-sided and ignored [[ethical responsibility]] in its pursuit.<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=29}} Starting in 1947 she was a contributor behind the scenes to the [[Godesberg Program|Bad Godesberg Programme]], prepared under the leadership of Eichler and issued in 1959, which provided a detailed modernising platform that carried the party into government in the 1960s.<ref name=":6" />

Hermann was the head of central office<ref name=":8" />{{Reference page|page=31}}for the [[Education and Science Workers' Union (Germany)|Education and Science Workers' Union]] from 1953 until 1965.<ref name=":12" /> During this time, Specht had also returned to Germany, where she became the head of the [[Odenwaldschule]] in [[Heppenheim]]<ref name="inge">Dr. [[Inge Hansen-Schaberg]], [http://www.philosophisch-politische-akademie.de/specht_e.html#top ''Erinnerung an Minna Specht''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081021050808/http://www.philosophisch-politische-akademie.de/specht_e.html|date=21 October 2008}} Philosophical-Political Academy. Lecture on memories of Minna Specht at the opening of an exhibit at Rhinbek castle. Retrieved 19 July 2010 {{in lang|de}}</ref> and chair of the {{Ill|Philosophisch-Politische Akademie|de}} (PPA),<ref name="fes2">[https://library.fes.de/fulltext/adsd/01412b.htm#E11E48 Grete Henry-Hermann] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220429194224/http://library.fes.de/fulltext/adsd/01412b.htm#E11E48 |date=29 April 2022 }}, Friedrich Ebert Foundation, downloaded 22 January 2012</ref> an organisation founded by Nelson in 1922, oriented towards education, social justice, responsible political action and its philosophical basis.<ref name=":9" /> When Specht retired in 1954, she removed to [[Bremen]] with Hermann. They resided together until Specht's death in 1961, after which time Hermann withdrew from public life, rarely appearing in public,<ref name=":12" /> and assumed leadership of PPA.<ref name="fes">[https://library.fes.de/fulltext/adsd/01412b.htm#E11E48 Grete Henry-Hermann] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220429194224/http://library.fes.de/fulltext/adsd/01412b.htm#E11E48 |date=29 April 2022 }}, Friedrich Ebert Foundation, downloaded 22 January 2012</ref> While there, she retired from her teaching post<ref name=":9" /> to focus entirely on critical philosophical thought<ref name=":12" /> and oversaw the posthumous publication of Nelson's works<ref name=":9" /> until 1978.<ref name="fes" /> 

Hermann died in April 1984 in Bremen.<ref name=":8" />
